subject: Behavioral Economics
title: Sunk Cost Trap
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Sunk Cost Trap.

hook.text: You sit through a terrible movie because you paid for the ticket. The money is gone either way.

buildup.text: Sunk costs are past expenses that cannot be recovered. Rationally, they should not affect future choices.

discovery.text: But we feel that quitting wastes the investment. So we invest more to justify what we already lost.

twist.text: The Concorde jet continued for decades despite losses. Governments kept funding to avoid admitting the sunk cost.

climax.text: Ask: if I had not already invested, would I start this now? If no, the sunk cost is trapping you. Walk away.

punchline.text: The money is gone. The only question is what to do next.

quiz.question: What is the sunk cost trap?
options: Avoiding all investments to prevent loss
Continuing a losing course because of past investment that can't be recovered
Accurately calculating total investment before deciding

details.summary: The sunk cost trap causes people to continue investing in a losing proposition because they have already invested money, time, or effort. Rational decision-making should consider only future costs and benefits, but sunk costs create emotional pressure to continue.
details.whyItMatters: Sunk cost reasoning wastes resources across all domains: staying in bad relationships, continuing failed projects, and sitting through terrible movies because you paid for the ticket. Past costs should not influence future decisions.
takeaways: Past investments should not influence decisions about future actions
People continue failing courses of action to avoid wasting previous investment
The rational question is always: given where I am now, what is the best path forward

faq.question: Why is it so hard to walk away from sunk costs?
faq.answer: Abandoning an investment means admitting loss, which triggers loss aversion. It also means admitting the original decision was wrong, which threatens self-image. These emotional pressures are powerful enough to override rational cost-benefit analysis.

faq.question: What is the best mental reframe to escape the sunk cost trap?
faq.answer: Ask: if I had not already invested in this, would I start it now based on the future prospects alone? If the answer is no, continuing is irrational regardless of what was already spent. This reframe separates past from future.
